questions.stem: Indirect form: He said, 'I am happy.'

options.option_text: He said that I am happy
He said that he was happy
He says that he is happy
He said that he is happy

questions.explanation: Reporting verb past → back-shift: am → was; pronoun I → he. Also drop the comma+quotes and add 'that'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Indirect form: She said, 'I will come tomorrow.'

options.option_text: She said that she will come tomorrow
She said that she would come the next day
She said that she will come the next day
She said that she came the next day

questions.explanation: will → would; tomorrow → the next day. These time shifts are systematic: today → that day, yesterday → the previous day, now → then, here → there.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Indirect form: He said, 'Where are you going?'

options.option_text: He said where I am going
He asked where I was going
He asked that where I was going
He asked where was I going

questions.explanation: Wh-question: (a) reporting verb changes 'said' → 'asked', (b) NO 'that' conjunction, (c) word order becomes statement order (subject before verb), (d) tense back-shifts.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Indirect form: She asked, 'Do you speak French?'

options.option_text: She asked that do I speak French
She asked whether I spoke French
She asked did I speak French
She asked I speak French

questions.explanation: Yes/No question → use 'if' or 'whether'; statement word order; tense back-shifts.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Indirect form: The teacher said, 'Don't make noise.'

options.option_text: The teacher said that don't make noise
The teacher asked us not to make noise
The teacher told that not to make noise
The teacher said us not to make noise

questions.explanation: Imperative (command/request) → reporting verb 'ordered / asked / requested / told'; reported clause uses 'to + V' (or 'not to + V' for negatives).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Indirect form: He said, 'How beautiful the flower is!'

options.option_text: He said that the flower is beautiful
He exclaimed that the flower was very beautiful
He exclaimed how beautiful was the flower
He said the flower was beautiful!

questions.explanation: Exclamation → reporting verb 'exclaimed / cried out'; convert 'how + adj' to 'very + adj'; add 'that'; drop exclamation mark.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct indirect speech. He said, 'I am reading a book.'

options.option_text: He said that he was reading a book.
He said that he is reading a book.
He told that he was reading a book.
He said that he had read a book.

questions.explanation: Present continuous 'am reading' shifts to past continuous 'was reading' in indirect speech. 'Said' (no object) is retained — 'told' requires an object ('told me/him'). 'He said that he had read' (past perfect) is wrong: past perfect is used when the direct speech was already past tense.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct indirect speech. She said to me, 'You are wrong.'

options.option_text: She told me that I was wrong.
She told me that you were wrong.
She said me that I was wrong.
She told me that I am wrong.

questions.explanation: 'Said to me' → 'told me'. The pronoun 'you' changes to 'I' (listener becomes subject). 'Are' → 'was' (tense backshift). 'Said me' is ungrammatical — 'said' cannot directly take a personal object. 'I am wrong' fails: tense must shift.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Convert to indirect speech. The teacher said, 'Do not make noise.'

options.option_text: The teacher told them not to make noise.
The teacher said not to make noise.
The teacher asked them do not make noise.
The teacher told them to not make noises.

questions.explanation: Imperative negatives use 'told [object] not to + bare infinitive.' 'Said not to' is possible but incomplete — it lacks the object ('them'). 'Asked them do not' is ungrammatical. 'Told them to not make noises' changes the number of 'noise' incorrectly.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct indirect speech. He asked, 'Can you help me?'

options.option_text: He asked if I could help him.
He asked if you could help him.
He asked whether I can help him.
He asked me if I can help him.

questions.explanation: 'Can' → 'could' (modal backshift). 'You' → 'I' (pronoun shift: the listener was 'you' in the direct speech, becomes the 'I' narrating). 'Me' → 'him' (object pronoun shift). 'Can help him' fails tense backshift. 'You could help him' fails pronoun shift.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Convert to indirect speech. Ravi said, 'I will come here tomorrow.'

options.option_text: Ravi said that he would come there the next day.
Ravi said that he will come here tomorrow.
Ravi told that he would come here the next day.
Ravi said that he would come there tomorrow.

questions.explanation: Key shifts: 'will' → 'would'; 'I' → 'he'; 'here' → 'there'; 'tomorrow' → 'the next day'. All four must change. Option B retains 'will/here/tomorrow' — triple error. Option C uses 'told that' — 'told' requires a named object, not 'that'. Option D retains 'tomorrow' instead of 'the next day'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Convert to indirect speech. Mother said to him, 'Have your meals on time.'

options.option_text: Mother advised him to have his meals on time.
Mother told him to have your meals on time.
Mother told him have his meals on time.
Mother said him to have his meals on time.

questions.explanation: Affirmative imperatives use 'advised/told/asked [object] to + infinitive.' 'Your' must shift to 'his.' 'Told him to have his' is correct but 'advised' is preferred for a caring instruction. 'Have his meals' (no 'to') is ungrammatical. 'Said him' is always wrong — 'said' cannot take a personal object directly.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Convert to indirect speech. She said, 'I have finished the work.'

options.option_text: She said that she had finished the work.
She said that she has finished the work.
She told that she had finished the work.
She said that she finished the work.

questions.explanation: Present perfect 'have finished' → past perfect 'had finished' in indirect speech after a past reporting verb. 'Has finished' retains the present perfect — wrong. 'Told that' is ungrammatical — needs a personal object. 'Finished' (simple past) is a possible conversion in some contexts, but 'had finished' is the standard and correct backshift here.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct indirect speech. He exclaimed, 'What a beautiful painting!'

options.option_text: He exclaimed that it was a very beautiful painting.
He exclaimed what a beautiful painting it was.
He said that what a beautiful painting.
He exclaimed that it is a very beautiful painting.

questions.explanation: Exclamatory sentences → 'exclaimed that + assertive sentence.' 'What a beautiful' transforms to 'very beautiful.' 'Was' (past tense backshift after past 'exclaimed'). Option B retains the exclamatory structure — wrong in standard indirect form. Option C uses 'said that what' — ungrammatical. Option D fails tense backshift ('is' should be 'was').
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Convert to indirect speech. The student said to the teacher, 'May I come in?'

options.option_text: The student asked the teacher if he might come in.
The student asked the teacher if he may come in.
The student requested the teacher may he come in.
The student said the teacher if he might come in.

questions.explanation: 'May' (permission/request) → 'might' in indirect speech after a past reporting verb. 'Said to [person]' becomes 'asked [person].' 'May I' → 'if he might' (pronoun shift + modal shift). Option B keeps 'may' — no backshift. Option C ('requested... may he') is ungrammatical. Option D uses 'said the teacher' — wrong preposition structure.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Convert to direct speech. He told me that he had been waiting for two hours.

options.option_text: He said to me, 'I have been waiting for two hours.'
He said to me, 'I had been waiting for two hours.'
He told me, 'I have been waiting for two hours.'
He said to me, 'I was waiting for two hours.'

questions.explanation: Reversing indirect to direct: past perfect continuous 'had been waiting' → present perfect continuous 'have been waiting.' The reporting verb reverts: 'told me' → 'said to me.' Option B retains 'had been' — wrong (that's past perfect, not present perfect continuous). Option C uses 'told me,' in direct speech, but 'told + quoted speech' is non-standard. Option D uses simple past continuous — loses the duration emphasis.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Identify the error in indirect speech conversion. Direct: She said, 'I bought this dress yesterday.' Indirect: She said that she had bought that dress the previous day.

options.option_text: No error — the conversion is correct.
'Yesterday' should stay as 'yesterday,' not 'the previous day.'
'Bought' should not shift to 'had bought' here.
'This' should remain 'this,' not change to 'that.'

questions.explanation: All three changes are correct: (1) 'bought' → 'had bought' (simple past → past perfect); (2) 'this' → 'that' (demonstrative shift); (3) 'yesterday' → 'the previous day' (time-adverb shift). This is a 'spot the correct conversion' trap — all changes look aggressive, but each follows a standard rule.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Convert to indirect speech. He said, 'Would that I were a king!'

options.option_text: He wished that he were a king.
He said that he would be a king.
He wished that he had been a king.
He exclaimed that he wished he were a king.

questions.explanation: 'Would that + subjunctive' is a wish construction. Indirect: 'wished that + subjunctive.' The subjunctive 'were' is retained (not shifted further to 'had been') because it already expresses an unreal present wish. 'Would be a king' loses the wish/unreal nuance. 'Had been' converts an unreal present to an unreal past — incorrect. Option D double-tags the reporting verb.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Convert to indirect speech. The manager said to the team, 'Work harder and you will succeed.'

options.option_text: The manager told the team to work harder and that they would succeed.
The manager told the team that work harder and they would succeed.
The manager told the team to work harder and would succeed.
The manager said the team to work harder and they will succeed.

questions.explanation: This is a conditional imperative: 'Do X and you will Y' → 'told [object] to do X and that they would Y.' The imperative part uses 'to + infinitive'; the result clause uses 'that + would + verb.' Option B inserts 'that' before 'work' — ungrammatical. Option C drops 'they' from the result clause. Option D uses 'said the team' (wrong) and 'will' (no backshift).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the best indirect speech form. She said to him, 'How dare you insult me!'

options.option_text: She angrily asked him how he dared to insult her.
She said that how dare he insult her.
She exclaimed how he dared to insult her.
She told him how dare he insult her.

questions.explanation: 'How dare you' is a rhetorical exclamation of indignation. It converts to 'asked [person] how [pronoun] dared to [verb].' 'Said to' → 'asked' (the emotion tag 'angrily' is correct but not obligatory). 'Said that how dare' is ungrammatical. 'Exclaimed how he dared' omits the object. 'Told him how dare' uses an imperative structure incorrectly.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Convert to indirect speech. He said, 'Let us begin the meeting now.'

options.option_text: He proposed that they should begin the meeting then.
He said that let us begin the meeting now.
He suggested them to begin the meeting then.
He proposed that they began the meeting then.

questions.explanation: 'Let us' (suggestion including the speaker) → 'proposed/suggested that they should + base verb.' 'Now' → 'then.' 'Said that let us' retains direct speech structure — wrong. 'Suggested them to begin' is wrong ('suggested' doesn't take 'to + infinitive' in standard grammar). 'They began' in option D uses simple past instead of 'should begin.'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Convert to indirect speech. He said, 'I have been living here since 2015.'

options.option_text: He said that he had been living there since 2015.
He said that he has been living here since 2015.
He said that he had been living there from 2015.
He said that he was living there since 2015.

questions.explanation: Present perfect continuous → past perfect continuous ('had been living'). 'Here' → 'there.' 'Since 2015' is retained (it refers to a specific year, not a relative time expression like 'yesterday' that must change). Option B keeps present perfect — wrong. Option C changes 'since' to 'from' — incorrect: 'since' with a point in time is retained. Option D uses simple past continuous — loses the perfect aspect.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct indirect form. She said to her friend, 'Happy Birthday!'

options.option_text: She wished her friend a happy birthday.
She said her friend happy birthday.
She told her friend to have a happy birthday.
She exclaimed happy birthday to her friend.

questions.explanation: Greeting/wish expressions convert to 'wished [object] + noun phrase.' 'Said her friend happy birthday' — 'said' cannot take two objects in this structure. 'Told her friend to have' adds an imperative that wasn't in the original. 'Exclaimed happy birthday' — exclaim needs a 'that/how/what' clause.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Convert to indirect speech. He said, 'If I were rich, I would travel the world.'

options.option_text: He said that if he were rich, he would travel the world.
He said that if he was rich, he would travel the world.
He said that if he had been rich, he would have travelled the world.
He said that if he were rich, he will travel the world.

questions.explanation: Hypothetical present conditions ('if + were + would') do NOT shift in indirect speech because the subjunctive 'were' already expresses unreality. The tense stays: 'were' and 'would travel' are retained. Option B uses 'was' — subjunctive 'were' must not be weakened to indicative 'was.' Option C shifts to past perfect — treats the condition as a past unreal event (incorrect). Option D changes 'would' to 'will' — backshift error.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Convert to indirect speech. The officer said to the soldiers, 'Stand at ease!'

options.option_text: The officer commanded the soldiers to stand at ease.
The officer told the soldiers stand at ease.
The officer said that stand at ease.
The officer ordered the soldiers standing at ease.

questions.explanation: Military commands use 'commanded/ordered [object] to + base verb.' 'Told... stand' omits 'to.' 'Said that stand' retains direct imperative form. 'Ordered... standing' uses wrong verb form (gerund instead of infinitive). Both 'commanded' and 'ordered' are acceptable here.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Which option correctly converts this to direct speech? The guide told the tourists that they must not touch the exhibits.

options.option_text: The guide said to the tourists, 'You must not touch the exhibits.'
The guide said to the tourists, 'You should not touch the exhibits.'
The guide said to the tourists, 'You can not touch the exhibits.'
The guide said to the tourists, 'Do not touch the exhibits.'

questions.explanation: 'Must not' in indirect speech converts back to 'must not' in direct speech — 'must' does not backshift (it has no past form). Option B substitutes 'should' — changes the force. Option C uses 'can not' — different modal. Option D converts to imperative, which would give the indirect form 'told them not to touch' — not 'must not touch.'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct indirect speech. She said, 'Alas! I have lost my purse.'

options.option_text: She exclaimed sorrowfully that she had lost her purse.
She exclaimed that alas she has lost her purse.
She said that she had lost her purse.
She exclaimed sorrowfully that she has lost her purse.

questions.explanation: 'Alas!' signals sorrow — the reporting verb uses 'exclaimed sorrowfully.' The interjection is dropped; the emotion is conveyed through the adverb. 'Have lost' → 'had lost' (tense backshift). Option B retains 'alas' and uses 'has' — both wrong. Option C drops the emotion entirely ('said' is too neutral). Option D correctly uses 'exclaimed sorrowfully' but retains 'has' (no backshift).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Convert to indirect speech. She said, 'I must finish this project today.'

options.option_text: She said that she had to finish that project that day.
She said that she must finish that project that day.
She said that she must finish this project today.
She said that she should finish that project that day.

questions.explanation: 'Must' (obligation) shifts to 'had to' in indirect speech when the context is past. 'Today' → 'that day'; 'this' → 'that.' Option B keeps 'must' — 'must' can stay in indirect speech only when it retains present necessity; here the sense is obligation that shifts. Option C keeps both 'must' and 'this/today.' Option D uses 'should' — different shade of meaning.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Convert to indirect speech. He said to her, 'What time did you reach home last night?'

options.option_text: He asked her what time she had reached home the previous night.
He asked her what time did she reach home last night.
He asked her what time she reached home last night.
He asked her what time had she reached home the previous night.

questions.explanation: WH-indirect questions use 'asked [object] + wh-word + subject + verb' (no auxiliary inversion). 'Did you reach' → 'she had reached' (simple past shifts to past perfect; subject-verb order, no 'did'). 'Last night' → 'the previous night.' Option B keeps question word-order ('did she reach') — wrong in indirect. Option C keeps 'last night' and retains simple past. Option D inverts 'had she' — auxiliary inversion is wrong in indirect speech.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Convert to indirect speech. He said, 'God save the Queen!'

options.option_text: He prayed that God might save the Queen.
He said that God saved the Queen.
He wished that God would save the Queen.
He prayed that God saves the Queen.

questions.explanation: Optative sentences (prayers/wishes with subjunctive) → 'prayed/wished that [subject] might + verb.' 'God save' is subjunctive (no -s). Indirect: 'prayed that God might save.' Option B converts to simple past declarative — wrong (drops the prayer force). Option C uses 'would' — 'might' is more appropriate for prayers. Option D retains present indicative 'saves' — no tense shift and wrong form.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Convert to indirect speech. He said, 'I don't know whether she will come or not.'

options.option_text: He said that he did not know whether she would come or not.
He said that he doesn't know whether she will come or not.
He said that he did not know whether she comes or not.
He said that he did not know if she would come or not.

questions.explanation: 'Don't know' → 'did not know'; 'will come' → 'would come'; 'whether...or not' is retained. Option B keeps present tense throughout — no backshift. Option C changes 'will' to 'comes' (present simple) — incorrect. Option D substitutes 'if' for 'whether... or not' — 'whether...or not' must remain 'whether...or not'; 'if' alone cannot carry the 'or not' structure.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Convert to indirect speech. He said to me, 'If you had studied harder, you would have passed.'

options.option_text: He told me that if I had studied harder, I would have passed.
He told me that if I studied harder, I would have passed.
He told me that if I had studied harder, I would pass.
He told me that if I had studied harder, I would have been passed.

questions.explanation: Type 3 conditionals (past unreal: 'had + V3, would have + V3') do NOT shift because they are already in the most remote past. Both clauses retain their forms. Option B changes 'had studied' to 'studied' — drops the past perfect. Option C changes 'would have passed' to 'would pass' — drops the perfect aspect. Option D uses 'been passed' — passive construction is wrong here ('pass' is intransitive in this sense).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correctly converted indirect speech. She said to the children, 'Never tell a lie, for honesty is the best policy.'

options.option_text: She advised the children never to tell a lie, adding that honesty is the best policy.
She told the children never to tell a lie and that honesty was the best policy.
She advised the children not to tell a lie and that honesty is the best policy.
She advised the children to never tell lies, for honesty is the best policy.

questions.explanation: Two clauses: (1) imperative + (2) a universal truth. The imperative converts to 'advised never to tell a lie.' Universal truths ('honesty is the best policy') are EXEMPT from tense shift — they remain in present tense. 'Adding that' or 'saying that' correctly introduces the universal truth. Option B uses 'was' — wrong for a universal truth. Option C uses 'not to tell' (less idiomatic than 'never to tell') and is otherwise acceptable, but omits the 'adding that' nuance. Option D splits the infinitive unnecessarily and retains 'for' from direct speech.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Convert to indirect speech. He said, 'I wish I could speak French.'

options.option_text: He expressed a wish that he could speak French.
He said that he wished he could speak French.
He said that he wished he can speak French.
He wished that he had spoken French.

questions.explanation: 'I wish + could' is a present unreal wish (no shift needed for 'could' since it's already modal past). The standard conversion is 'expressed a wish that + subject + could.' Option B 'he wished he could speak' is also acceptable and widely accepted — this question tests awareness that 'expressed a wish' is the most precise form. Option C changes 'could' to 'can' — wrong (no backshift reversal). Option D converts to a past unreal wish — changes the meaning.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: He said, 'The Earth revolves around the Sun.' The correct indirect form is:

options.option_text: He said that the Earth revolves around the Sun.
He said that the Earth revolved around the Sun.
He said that the Earth had revolved around the Sun.
He told that the Earth revolves around the Sun.

questions.explanation: Universal/scientific truths are exempt from tense backshift. 'Revolves' stays in present simple regardless of the past reporting verb. Option B applies tense shift — wrong for a scientific fact. Option C shifts to past perfect — doubly wrong. Option D uses 'told that' — 'told' needs a personal object.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Convert to indirect speech. He said to his son, 'May you succeed in life!'

options.option_text: He blessed his son, wishing that he might succeed in life.
He told his son that he may succeed in life.
He wished his son to succeed in life.
He said to his son that he might succeed in life.

questions.explanation: 'May you' (blessing/prayer) → 'blessed [person], wishing that [pronoun] might.' 'May' → 'might' (modal backshift). Option B uses 'told that... may' — wrong modal and wrong reporting verb. Option C ('wished... to succeed') drops the 'might' and converts to an infinitive — loses the blessing tone. Option D ('said to... might') uses the wrong reporting verb ('said to' → should be 'blessed'/'prayed') and doesn't reflect the blessing context.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Find the error. Direct: 'Who are you?' he asked. Indirect (as written): He asked who I was.

options.option_text: No error — the conversion is correct.
Should be: He asked who was I.
Should be: He asked who am I.
Should be: He asked who I am.

questions.explanation: WH-indirect questions place the subject before the verb with no inversion: 'who I was' — correct. 'Are' → 'was' (backshift from present to past; 'you' → 'I'). Option B inverts ('who was I') — wrong in indirect speech. Option C retains present tense and inversion — both wrong. Option D retains 'am' (no backshift) — wrong.
questions.subject: English
